summary: A 1971 proposal by Steve Crocker for a network standard format for a data stream controlling a graphics display. It was updated by RFC 125.

plainLanguage.summary: A proposal for a common way to send drawing instructions over the network to a screen.

subtitle: A 1971 sketch of a standard stream of drawing commands for remote graphics displays.

tldr.problem: A user at a local console who works on a remote Host needs the remote program's output drawn on a refresh display with point, vector and character capability, and every site would otherwise do this differently.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal postulates a network standard display list and screen, plus a stream of just two commands, Erase and Replace, that rebuild the lists a display controller executes.
tldr.outcome: The author says it is illustrative only and meant as a basis for discussion. It was updated by RFC 125.

today: The unit metadata lists the status as unknown, and the RFC was updated by RFC 125. The text itself describes the proposal as illustrative and a basis for discussion.

sections.title: The Problem and the Model
sections.content:
In a typical setup, a console is attached to a computer at the user's site while the user works on a remote Host. This proposal covers the output stream when the console is a refresh display with point, vector and character drawing. It names the DEC 338, DEC 340, IBM 2250 and IMLAC PDS-1 as devices in that class.

Steve Crocker states that the proposal is illustrative only and knowingly avoids important issues. Its main purpose is to give a basis for discussion. To define the meaning of the network standard graphics data stream (NGDS) he postulates a display list (NGDL), a stream interpreter (NGSI), a list interpreter or display controller (NGLI) and a screen (NGS).
sections.plainLanguage: The remote computer sends drawing instructions. A helper at your end turns them into a to-do list, and the screen follows that list over and over.

sections.title: The Screen and the Display List
sections.content:
The NGS is square, and a position on it is an ordered pair of unsigned 16 bit fractions: horizontal distance from the left edge, then vertical distance from the bottom edge. Resolution is deliberately left unspecified, so picture quality should degrade gradually on lower-resolution displays. Characters are assumed to be at most .015 screen width wide and .025 screen height high, which gives 67 characters to a line and 40 lines. The character set is ASCII without form control characters, but including space.

The NGDL is a set of named, possibly empty lists. Names are 16 bit integers, and name zero is the chief list. Each item in a list is one of five kinds: move the beam, display a vector, display the current point, display n characters, or execute another list with a given origin. The NGLI loops forever over the chief list, whose origin is always 0,0, and the last kind of item works like a subroutine call, so the interpreter is recursive.
sections.plainLanguage: The screen is a square sheet. The to-do list can say move, draw a line, put a dot, write letters, or go do another little list first and then come back.

sections.title: The Data Stream Commands
sections.content:
The NGSI parses the stream into commands in prefix form: an eight bit operation code followed by any arguments. Each command is executed as soon as it is recognized. Only two commands are defined.

Erase is a single zero-valued opcode with no arguments, and it makes every list null, which erases the screen. Replace has opcode 1, a 16-bit list name and an 8 bit subargument count, followed by that many subarguments. It deletes all items from the named list and rebuilds it from the subarguments. There are five kinds of subargument matching the five item types, coded as the 8 bit values 0 to 4.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only two orders: wipe everything, or throw away one list and write it again from scratch.
